chapterTitle: Ch 13. Neural Networks as Distribution Transformers

concepts.title: Checkpoint
concepts.one_liner: A checkpoint is a record of the parameter vector at a specific iteration of the training process.
concepts.content: A checkpoint is a record of the parameters at some iteration of training. Specifically, if the iterates of the parameter vector are $\theta^0, \theta^1, \ldots, \theta^T$, then any $\theta^k$ can be recorded as a checkpoint.
concepts.motivation_md: Checkpoints allow researchers and practitioners to save the state of a model during training, enabling them to resume training later, evaluate performance at different stages, or recover from system failures.
concepts.recap_md: - A checkpoint captures the parameter vector $\theta^k$ at a specific training step $k$.

key_passage.text: A checkpoint is a record of the parameters at some iteration of training, that is, if iterates of the parameter vector are $\theta^0, \theta^1, \ldots, \theta^T$, then any $\theta^k$ can be recorded as a checkpoint.

concepts.title: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE)

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

concepts.one_liner: t-SNE is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while preserving relative distances between points.
concepts.content:
t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a dimensionality reduction tool used to visualize high-dimensional data and activations by projecting them to a lower dimensionality, such as 2D. A common objective of this projection is to ensure that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space.

In the following plot, (see figure: How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer...), t-SNE is used to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset of images. While the original embeddings are high-dimensional (for example, 38,400-dimensional), t-SNE maps them down to 2D. This visualization provides a rough view of the network's internal representations, showing how semantic classes (represented by different colors) are separated across layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep learning representations are typically high-dimensional, making them impossible to visualize directly. t-SNE solves this by projecting these representations into 2D or 3D while maintaining the local structure of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - t-SNE projects high-dimensional embeddings into 2D for visualization purposes.

key_passage.text: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding. t-SNE to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset of images of different semantic classes, where each color represents a different semantic class.

concepts.title: Dimensionality reduction

position.section_title: How High-Dimensional Datapoints Get Remapped by Deep Net

concepts.one_liner: Dimensionality reduction tools project high-dimensional data to a lower-dimensional space, typically for visualization or analysis.
concepts.content: Dimensionality reduction refers to a set of tools that project high-dimensional data, such as deep net activations, to a lower dimensionality (for example, 2D) so that it can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the lower-dimensional projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the original high-dimensional space. Examples of this technique include t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), which can map embeddings from tens of thousands of dimensions down to 2D to provide a rough view of how a network represents data.
concepts.motivation_md: Since humans cannot perceive more than three dimensions, dimensionality reduction is essential for interpreting the complex, high-dimensional feature spaces learned by neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Projects high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional (e.g., 2D) spaces.

key_passage.text: These tools project the high-dimensional data to a lower dimensionality, for example 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space.

concepts.title: Disentangled Representation
concepts.one_liner: Disentangled representation occurs when a network reorganizes data so that different semantic classes become cleanly separated in representational space.
concepts.content: Layer by layer, deep nets transform data from its raw format to ever more abstracted and useful representations. This process can be viewed as a set of geometric transformations or as a kind of disentangling where initially messy data gets reorganized so that different data classes become cleanly separated. In a disentangled representation, each semantic class occupies a different part of the representational space. This is often observed in the final layers of a network, especially if the network has been trained to output a direct representation of semantics, such as through contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP).
concepts.motivation_md: Raw data is often 'tangled,' with different classes overlapping in complex ways. Disentangling these classes into distinct regions of space makes it easier for the model to perform classification or downstream tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Deep nets transform raw data into abstracted, disentangled representations.

concepts.title: Neural Networks as Distribution Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Deep networks can be viewed as stacks of functions that perform geometric transformations on data distributions.
concepts.content: Deep nets are stacks of simple functions which compose to achieve interesting mappings from inputs to outputs. A useful way of thinking about deep nets is to view each layer as a geometric transformation of a data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing neural networks as distribution transformers helps visualize how complex data is reshaped and simplified as it passes through the layers of a model.
concepts.recap_md: - Each layer acts as a geometric transformation of the data distribution.

key_passage.text: The idea is to think of each layer as a geometric transformation of a data distribution.

motivation.text: So far we have seen that deep nets are stacks of simple functions, which compose to achieve interesting mappings from inputs to outputs. This section will introduce a slightly different way of thinking about deep nets.

concepts.title: A Different Way of Plotting Functions

position.section_title: A Different Way of Plotting Functions

concepts.one_liner: Functions can be visualized as mappings that rearrange input space by plotting the output axis horizontally.
concepts.content:
Each layer in a deep net is a mapping from one representation of the data to another: $f: \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}} \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{\text{out}}$. If $\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}}$ are both one-dimensional (1D), we can consider a different way of plotting the mapping where we rotate the $y$-axis to be horizontal rather than vertical.

(see figure: The traditional way of plotting the function $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$.)

This depiction makes it obvious that functions are mappings that rearrange the input space.

(see figure: An alternative way of plotting a function. Functions are mappings that rearrange the input space. The identity function $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}}=\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$, shown here, means "no...)

The identity mapping $\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}}$ shows datapoints mapped to unchanged positions.

(see figure: Mapping plots for several simple functions that could be neural layers.)
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional function plots focus on the relationship between variables, but rotating the axes emphasizes how a function physically moves or 'warps' the space where data resides.

concepts.title: Deep networks as distribution transformers

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: Deep networks reshape data distributions layer by layer to match a target configuration, such as one-hot encoded labels.
concepts.content:
An incoming data distribution can be reshaped layer by layer into a desired configuration. For example, a binary softmax classifier moves class 0 points to $(1,0)$ and class 1 points to $(0,1)$ on the output layer, corresponding to their one-hot codes. A deep net stacks these operations.

(see figure: Mapping plot for a `linear`-`relu` stack.)

We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ into an output data distribution $p_{\text {out}}$. Each layer of activations is a different representation or embedding of the data, denoted as $p_{\ell}$ for layer $\ell$. Layer by layer, the net transforms $p_{\text {data }}$ into $p_{\texttt{1}}$, then $p_{\texttt{2}}$, and so on. Most loss functions penalize the divergence between the resulting output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective explains the 'work' a neural network does: it iteratively warps the geometry of the data until the different classes or values are easily separable or identifiable by the final layer.
concepts.recap_md: - Deep nets transform an input distribution $p_{\text{data}}$ into an output distribution $p_{\text{out}}$ through successive layers.

key_passage.text: We can think of a deep net as transforming an input data distribution, $p_{\text{data}}$, into an output data distribution, $p_{\text{out}}$. Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or embedding of the data, and we can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. Then, layer by layer, a deep net transforms $p_{\text{data}}$ into $p_{\texttt{1}}$ into $p_{\texttt{2}}$, and so on until finally transforming the data to the distribution $p_{\text{out}}$.

motivation.text: Most loss functions can also be interpreted from this angle: they penalize the divergence, in one form or another, between the output distribution $p_{\text{out}}$ and a target distribution $p_{\texttt{target}}$.

concepts.title: Embedding

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: An embedding is a representation of data at a specific layer of activations within a neural network.
concepts.content: Each layer of activations in a network is a different representation or **embedding** of the data. We can consider the distribution of activations on some layer $\ell$ to be $p_{\ell}$. A deep net transforms the input data distribution $p_{\text {data }}$ layer by layer through these embeddings until it reaches the final output distribution $p_{\text {out}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Embeddings allow the network to translate raw input into a more useful, structured space where the relevant features for the task are highlighted.
concepts.recap_md: - An embedding refers to the internal representation of data at a specific layer.

concepts.title: Sparsity in ReLU networks

position.section_title: How Deep Nets Remap a Data Distribution

concepts.one_liner: ReLU layers induce sparsity by mapping large portions of the high-dimensional embedding space onto the axes.
concepts.content:
Visualizing 2D-to-2D mappings provides insight into how neural net layers transform data. 

(see figure: 2D mapping diagrams for several neural layers. The `linear` layer mapping will shift, stretch, and rotate depending on its weights and biases.)

A ReLU layer maps many points to the axes of the positive quadrant. In high-dimensional embeddings, this effect is exaggerated. For a width-$N$ layer, the strictly positive region occupies only $\frac{1}{2^N}$ proportion of the embedding space; consequently, almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes. This leads to sparse high-dimensional neural representations where most of the representational volume is unoccupied by datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding sparsity helps explain how ReLU networks compress information and why high-dimensional representations often reside on low-dimensional manifolds.
concepts.recap_md: - ReLU layers map any point not in the positive quadrant to an axis, creating data density along these boundaries.

key_passage.text: In particular, for a width-N layer, the region that is strictly positive occupies only 1/2^N proportion of the embedding space, so almost the entire space gets mapped to the axes after a relu layer. The geometry of high-dimensional neural representations may become very sparse because of this, where most of the volume of representational space is not occupied by any datapoints.

motivation.text: One interesting thing to notice here is that the relu layer maps many points to the axes of the positive quadrant. In general, with relu-nets, a lot of data density will build up along these axes, because any point not in the positive quadrant snaps to an axis.

prereq.rationale: This concept builds on the general idea of networks as transformers by detailing the layer-by-layer process of reshaping distributions.
The concept of an embedding is used to track the distribution's state through the layer-by-layer transformation process.
Sparsity is analyzed as a property of the high-dimensional embedding space where representations are formed.
Disentangling is explicitly described as a process of geometric transformations that reorganize data into a cleaner state.
The concept of disentanglement refers to how semantic classes are positioned relative to one another within the network's representational (embedding) space.
t-SNE is applied to high-dimensional embeddings (such as deep net activations) to make their structure interpretable to humans.

overlay.rationale: Both concepts deal with visualizing neural network operations as spatial transformations of data.
Sparsity is a concrete example of how a specific layer type (ReLU) reshapes a data distribution by pushing it onto axes.
Disentangled representation is a specific, high-level outcome of the general capacity of deep networks to transform data distributions.
Techniques like t-SNE are the primary tools used to visualize and confirm the clean separation of classes in the final layers of a network.
t-SNE is a specific, widely used algorithm for dimensionality reduction, particularly optimized for 2D or 3D visualization.
t-SNE provides a visual demonstration of how deep networks transform and disentangle input distributions across successive layers.
Dimensionality reduction is often the process used to visualize or compress high-dimensional embeddings.
Rotating the output axis provides a concrete visual demonstration of how a function 'rearranges' or transforms the input space, supporting the view of networks as transformers.
